skills.name: Electronic configuration and chemical properties: alkali metals and halogens

note.text:
Alkali metals (group I: Li, Na, K) have 1 valence electron, which they lose easily to form +1 ions.
• Soft, shiny when cut, stored under oil; react vigorously with water to give an alkaline hydroxide and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
• Reactivity increases down the group (the outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily): K > Na > Li.
Halogens (group VII: F, Cl, Br, I) have 7 valence electrons and gain 1 to form −1 ions (halide ions).
• Coloured, poisonous non-metals; diatomic molecules (Cl₂). Reactivity decreases down the group: F > Cl > Br > I.
• They react with alkali metals to form salts: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.

sections.heading: Group I: the alkali metals
sections.text:
Lithium, sodium and potassium have {1} electron in the outer shell. They react by losing it to form ions with a +{1} charge: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻.
They are soft (they can be cut with a knife), shiny when freshly cut, and so reactive that they are stored under oil.
With water they fizz, giving hydrogen gas and an alkaline solution of the hydroxide: {'2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂'}. That is why they are called alkali metals.

sections.heading: Reactivity down group I
sections.text:
Going down the group, atoms have more shells, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded. It is held less strongly and lost more easily.
So reactivity increases: lithium fizzes steadily, sodium melts into a ball and races around, potassium bursts into a lilac flame.

sections.heading: Group VII: the halogens
sections.text:
Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine have {7} outer electrons. They react by gaining {1} electron to form −{1} ions (fluoride, chloride, bromide, iodide).
They are coloured, poisonous non-metals made of pairs of atoms (Cl₂). Going down the group, the extra electron is attracted less strongly, so reactivity decreases: fluorine is the most reactive.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salts.

key_words.meaning: group VII: F, Cl, Br, I
a more reactive element pushing a less reactive one out of a compound

mistake.wrong: Halogens get more reactive down the group, like alkali metals
mistake.right: Halogen reactivity decreases down the group
mistake.why: Halogens gain an electron, and that is harder when the outer shell is further from the nucleus.

worked_example.problem: Explain why potassium reacts more vigorously with water than sodium.
steps: Both have {1} valence electron and react by losing it.
Potassium has more shells ({2}, {8}, {8}, {1}), so its outer electron is further from the nucleus.
It is held less strongly and lost more easily, so potassium is more reactive.
worked_example.answer: Its outer electron is further from the nucleus and is lost more easily

cards.idea: Alkali metals lose {1} electron to form +{1} ions; reactivity increases down the group.
Halogens gain {1} electron to form −{1} ions; reactivity decreases down the group.
Alkali metal + water → alkaline hydroxide + hydrogen.

Sodium is less reactive than potassium.

pick.q: What ion does an alkali metal form?
e: Metals lose electrons, making positive ions.
Group I has one electron to lose.

pick.y: Reactivity of halogens decreases down the group.

pick.q: What ion does a halogen form?
e: It gains only one electron to fill its shell.
pick.y: Seven outer electrons: gaining one fills the shell.

pick.q: Why does reactivity INCREASE down group I but DECREASE down group VII?
pick.r: Group I loses an electron (easier when far from the nucleus); group VII gains one (harder when far from the nucleus)
w: Atoms get smaller down both groups
e: Atoms get larger down a group.
Halogens are non-metals that gain electrons.
pick.y: Distance from the nucleus helps losing but hinders gaining.

pick.q: Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution and the solution turns orange. Why?
pick.r: Chlorine is more reactive and displaces bromine
e: The less reactive halogen cannot displace a more reactive one.
The orange colour shows bromine has formed.

pick.q: Rubidium is below potassium in group I. Predict its reaction with water.
e: It is lower in the group, so more reactive.
All alkali metals react with water.
